column1: What is the difference between locking and syncing?
column2: Locking decides one exact set of versions and writes it down. Syncing makes your folder match that decision.

column1: Do you normally run uv lock yourself?
column2: Rarely. uv add, uv run and uv sync all lock first, so the file stays current on its own.

column1: What does the hash field in uv.lock record?
column2: Which exact bytes, using sha256 — not merely which release.

column1: Why does a hash matter more than a version number?
column2: A version can in principle be re-uploaded, and downloads can be corrupted. A mismatch makes uv refuse to install.
One lockfile covers every platform and several Python versions, so a colleague on another operating system uses the same file.

column1: What is the default behaviour of uv sync?
column2: Exact. The environment is made to match the lockfile, and anything not recorded is removed.

column1: You pip-installed a package and then ran uv sync. What happens?
column2: uv uninstalls it, because it is not in the lockfile.

column1: How do you keep extra packages during a sync?

column2: Fails if the lockfile is out of date, which is what you want on a build machine.
Uses the lockfile exactly as it stands and never re-resolves.

column1: Does uv upgrade packages when a new release appears?
column2: No. New releases are ignored until you explicitly ask.

column1: When does a lockfile actually go stale?
column2: When a requirement changes so the locked version no longer qualifies. Loosening a constraint that still allows it does not.

column1: Which command checks whether the lockfile is current?

column2: Yes. It is what makes two machines identical, and it is plain text a review can read.

column1: Should uv.lock ever be edited by hand?
column2: No. It is generated output, and the next command will overwrite your edit.
pyproject says what your project can live with. uv.lock says what it actually got, down to the bytes.
